claim: Compartment formation in interphase chromosomes is a result of spatial segregation between euchromatin and heterochromatin on a few megabase pairs (Mbp) scale.
source: Compartment formation in interphase chromosomes is a result of spatial segregation between euchromatin and heterochromatin on a few megabase pairs (Mbp) scale.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about chromosome organization in the abstract.

claim: On the sub-Mbp scales, topologically associating domains (TADs) appear as interacting domains along the diagonal in the ensemble averaged Hi-C contact map.
source: On the sub-Mbp scales, topologically associating domains (TADs) appear as interacting domains along the diagonal in the ensemble averaged Hi-C contact map.
evidence: This describes the characteristic appearance of TADs in Hi-C data, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Hi-C experiments showed that most of the TADs vanish upon deleting cohesin, while the compartment structure is maintained, and perhaps even enhanced.
source: Hi-C experiments showed that most of the TADs vanish upon deleting cohesin, while the compartment structure is maintained, and perhaps even enhanced.
evidence: This refers to previous experimental findings from Hi-C studies.

claim: A non-negligible fraction of TADs is preserved (P-TADs) after cohesin loss.
source: However, closer inspection of the data reveals that a non-negligible fraction of TADs is preserved (P-TADs) after cohesin loss.
evidence: This is a key finding from the authors' analysis of Hi-C data.

claim: Imaging experiments show that, at the single-cell level, TAD-like structures are present even without cohesin.
source: Imaging experiments show that, at the single-cell level, TAD-like structures are present even without cohesin.
evidence: This refers to previous imaging studies showing TAD-like structures persist without cohesin.

claim: Certain TADs with epigenetic switches across their boundaries survive after depletion of loops.
source: To provide a structural basis for these findings, we first used polymer simulations to show that certain TADs with epigenetic switches across their boundaries survive after depletion of loops.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' polymer simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many of the P-TADs have sharp physical boundaries in three-dimensional structures.
source: More importantly, the three-dimensional structures show that many of the P-TADs have sharp physical boundaries.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of 3D structures.

claim: Epigenetic switches and physical boundaries explain the origin of the P-TADs in mouse liver and human colorectal carcinoma cell lines.
source: Informed by the simulations, we analyzed the Hi-C maps (with and without cohesin) in mouse liver and human colorectal carcinoma cell lines, which affirmed that epigenetic switches and physical boundaries (calculated using the predicted 3D structures using the data-driven HIPPS method that uses Hi-C as the input) explain the origin of the P-TADs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' analysis of experimental Hi-C data using the HIPPS method.

claim: Single-cell structures display TAD-like features in the absence of cohesin that are remarkably similar to the findings in imaging experiments.
source: Single-cell structures display TAD-like features in the absence of cohesin that are remarkably similar to the findings in imaging experiments.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' computational analysis that agrees with experimental imaging data.

claim: Some P-TADs, with physical boundaries, are relevant to the retention of enhancer–promoter/promoter–promoter interactions.
source: Some P-TADs, with physical boundaries, are relevant to the retention of enhancer–promoter/promoter–promoter interactions.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis connecting P-TADs to functional genomic interactions.

claim: Preservation of a subset of TADs upon removing cohesin is a robust phenomenon that is valid across multiple cell lines.
source: Overall, our study shows that preservation of a subset of TADs upon removing cohesin is a robust phenomenon that is valid across multiple cell lines.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' analysis across different cell types.

claim: Contacts are enriched within the TADs and are suppressed across the boundaries between the TADs.
source: Contacts are enriched within the TADs and are suppressed across the boundaries between the TADs.
evidence: This describes the defining characteristic of TADs in Hi-C contact maps.

claim: A number of polymer models (Barbieri et al., 2012; Di Pierro et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2018; Conte et al., 2020; Jost et al., 2014; Barbieri et al., 2017) have shown that compartment formations and TADs may be explained using micro-phase separation between A- and B-type loci.
source: A number of polymer models (Barbieri et al., 2012; Di Pierro et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2018; Conte et al., 2020; Jost et al., 2014; Barbieri et al., 2017) have shown that compartment formations and TADs may be explained using micro-phase separation between A- and B-type loci.
evidence: This summarizes findings from multiple previous polymer modeling studies.

claim: Recent Micro-C experiments have shown that there are fine structures starting from the nucleosome level (Hsieh et al., 2015; Hsieh et al., 2016; Hsieh et al., 2020), thus establishing the hierarchical organization of interphase chromosomes over a broad range of length scales.
source: In particular, recent Micro-C experiments have shown that there are fine structures starting from the nucleosome level (Hsieh et al., 2015; Hsieh et al., 2016; Hsieh et al., 2020), thus establishing the hierarchical organization of interphase chromosomes over a broad range of length scales.
evidence: This cites recent experimental findings about chromosome organization at fine scales.

claim: TADs are thought to regulate gene expression by constraining the contacts between target gene and regulatory regions (Dowen et al., 2014; Özdemir and Gambetta, 2019).
source: TADs are thought to regulate gene expression by constraining the contacts between target gene and regulatory regions (Dowen et al., 2014; Özdemir and Gambetta, 2019).
evidence: This describes the proposed functional role of TADs, citing previous work.

claim: Perturbation or disruption of TAD integrity such as deletions, duplications, or inversions of DNA segments within the TADs could lead to aberrant gene expression (Hnisz et al., 2016a; Szabo et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2016; Lupiáñez et al., 2015; Hnisz et al., 2016b; Rao et al., 2017; Ren and Dixon, 2015; Bianco et al., 2018).
source: As a consequence, perturbation or disruption of their integrity such as deletions, duplications, or inversions of DNA segments within the TADs could lead to aberrant gene expression (Hnisz et al., 2016a; Szabo et al., 2019; Ji et al., 2016; Lupiáñez et al., 2015; Hnisz et al., 2016b; Rao et al., 2017; Ren and Dixon, 2015; Bianco et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the consequences of TAD disruption, citing multiple previous studies.

claim: A class of chromatin loops, mediated by the ATP-dependent motor cohesin (Kim and Yu, 2020) and the DNA-binding protein CTCF protein ('cohesin-associated CTCF loop'), organizes a subset of the TADs (Fudenberg et al., 2016).
source: A class of chromatin loops, mediated by the ATP-dependent motor cohesin (Kim and Yu, 2020) and the DNA-binding protein CTCF protein ('cohesin-associated CTCF loop'), organizes a subset of the TADs (Fudenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the role of cohesin and CTCF in TAD organization, citing previous work.

claim: Cohesin (Kim and Yu, 2020) extrudes DNA loops of varying lengths, which are terminated when the motor encounters the transcriptional insulator CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) (Phillips and Corces, 2009).
source: It is thought that cohesin (Kim and Yu, 2020) extrudes DNA loops of varying lengths, which are terminated when the motor encounters the transcriptional insulator CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) (Phillips and Corces, 2009).
evidence: This describes the loop extrusion model for cohesin function, citing previous work.

claim: Cohesin and CTCF are often colocalized at the TAD boundary (Fudenberg et al., 2016; Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2015; Rao et al., 2014; Dekker et al., 2013; Vietri Rudan et al., 2015).
source: This implies that cohesin and CTCF are often colocalized at the TAD boundary (Fudenberg et al., 2016; Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2015; Rao et al., 2014; Dekker et al., 2013; Vietri Rudan et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the spatial relationship between cohesin, CTCF, and TAD boundaries, citing multiple studies.

claim: Several experiments have shown that depletion of the architectural proteins (Nipbl, RAD21, and CTCF) disrupts the organization of interphase chromosomes (Rao et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Nuebler et al., 2018; Wutz et al., 2017; Haarhuis et al., 2017; Nora et al., 2017; Zuin et al., 2014; Bintu et al., 2018; de Wit and Nora, 2023).
source: Several experiments have shown that depletion of the architectural proteins (Nipbl, RAD21, and CTCF) disrupts the organization of interphase chromosomes (Rao et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017; Nuebler et al., 2018; Wutz et al., 2017; Haarhuis et al., 2017; Nora et al., 2017; Zuin et al., 2014; Bintu et al., 2018; de Wit and Nora, 2023).
evidence: This summarizes findings from multiple experimental studies on the effects of depleting architectural proteins.

claim: Schwarzer et al., 2017 showed that the removal of the cohesin loading factor, Nipbl, in the mouse liver cell results in loss of TADs.
source: Schwarzer et al., 2017 showed that the removal of the cohesin loading factor, Nipbl, in the mouse liver cell results in loss of TADs.
evidence: This cites a specific finding from a previous experimental study.

claim: Compartment formation, which is independent of cohesin, is a consequence of the underlying epigenetic landscape, while TAD formation requires cohesin.
source: They concluded that compartment formation, which is independent of cohesin, is a consequence of the underlying epigenetic landscape, while TAD formation requires cohesin.
evidence: This summarizes conclusions from previous work about the different requirements for compartment and TAD formation.

claim: Upon removal of cohesin subunit RAD21 cohesin-associated CTCF loops and TADs are abolished (Rao et al., 2017; Zuin et al., 2014; Bintu et al., 2018).
source: Similarly, it was found that upon removal of cohesin subunit RAD21 cohesin-associated CTCF loops and TADs are abolished (Rao et al., 2017; Zuin et al., 2014; Bintu et al., 2018).
evidence: This cites findings from multiple studies on the effects of RAD21 deletion.

claim: Deletion of RAD21 results in the complete loss of the so-called loop domains (Rao et al., 2017), which are formed when CTCF colocalizes with cohesin.
source: Deletion of RAD21 results in the complete loss of the so-called loop domains (Rao et al., 2017), which are formed when CTCF colocalizes with cohesin.
evidence: This cites a specific finding about loop domains from a previous study.

claim: Imaging experiments (Bintu et al., 2018) showed that TAD-like structures, with sharp boundaries, at the single-cell level survive even after deleting cohesin.
source: In contrast, imaging experiments (Bintu et al., 2018) showed that TAD-like structures, with sharp boundaries, at the single-cell level survive even after deleting cohesin.
evidence: This cites a specific finding from an imaging study.

claim: Factors that prevent the association of cohesin with chromosomes globally abolish the TADs and the Hi-C peaks, but preserve (or even enhance) compartmentalization.
source: Factors that prevent the association of cohesin with chromosomes globally abolish the TADs and the Hi-C peaks, but preserve (or even enhance) compartmentalization.
evidence: This summarizes a key finding from multiple experimental and computational studies.

claim: Experimental studies (Schwarzer et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2014; Zuin et al., 2014; Bintu et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2017) and polymer simulations (Nuebler et al., 2018; Conte et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2020) have shown that the global epigenetic state determines compartment formation, while the more dynamic TADs, with finite lifetimes (Hansen et al., 2017), require ATP-dependent cohesin.
source: Experimental studies (Schwarzer et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2014; Zuin et al., 2014; Bintu et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2017) and polymer simulations (Nuebler et al., 2018; Conte et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2020) have shown that the global epigenetic state determines compartment formation, while the more dynamic TADs, with finite lifetimes (Hansen et al., 2017), require ATP-dependent cohesin.
evidence: This summarizes findings from multiple experimental and computational studies about the determinants of compartment and TAD formation.

claim: TAD-like features persist in single cells before and after auxin treatment, albeit with changes in the locations of the sharp domain boundaries.
source: TAD-like features persist in single cells before and after auxin treatment, albeit with changes in the locations of the sharp domain boundaries.
evidence: This summarizes findings from previous imaging experiments.

claim: Roughly 659 TADs out of 4176 (16%) are preserved after removing Nipbl in the mouse liver cells.
source: Using TopDom (Shin et al., 2016), we discovered that roughly 659 TADs out of 4176 (16%) are preserved (Figure 1a) after removing Nipbl in the mouse liver cells.

claim: In the HCT-116 cells, 1226 TADs out of 4733 (26%) are preserved upon RAD21 loss.
source: In the HCT-116 cells, 1226 TADs out of 4733 (26%) are preserved (Figure 1b) upon RAD21 loss.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' analysis of experimental Hi-C data, shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The number of P-TADs depends on the chromosome number.
source: Figure 1c and d show that the number of P-TADs depends on the chromosome number.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' analysis shown in Figure 1c and d.

claim: The CCM simulations reproduce the ubiquitous checkerboard patterns well.
source: The CCM simulations (Appendix 5—figure 2b) reproduce the ubiquitous checkerboard patterns well.

source: In the CCM simulations of chromosomes from the human GM12878 cell line, a subset of TADs remains even after deleting cohesin-associated CTCF loops (Figure 3a).

source: The percentages of P-TADs depend on both the resolution of the Hi-C experiments and the algorithm used to identify the TADs.

source: The results in Figure 3d and e show that a switch in the epigenetic state across a TAD boundary in the WT is likely to result in its preservation after cohesin-associated CTCF loop loss.

source: The physical boundaries of TAD-like domains, identified from individual 3D structures, vary from cell to cell.

source: These observations imply that the presence of physical boundaries in the 3D structures may be used to identify P-TADs, especially in instances when there are no epigenetic switches.

claim: The E–P and P–P loops are at the boundary of the TADs even in the absence of epigenetic switch, implying that it is a domain that is needed for E–P or P–P communication.
source: In the latter case, the E–P and P–P loops (blue circles) are at the boundary of the TADs even in the absence of epigenetic switch, implying that it is a domain that is needed for E–P or P–P communication.
evidence: This is an inference from the authors' analysis of Micro-C data, shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The TADs were also conserved upon cohesin loss.
source: Interestingly, the TADs were also conserved upon cohesin loss (right panel in Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of Micro-C data, shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The TADs with E–P/P–P loops have strong physical boundaries sans cohesin.
source: Analyses of the 3D structures (Figure 7b) reveal that the TADs with E–P/P–P loops have strong physical boundaries sans cohesin.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of 3D structures, shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Only a subset of TADs is conserved, potentially for functional reasons.
source: We propose that only a subset of TADs is conserved, potentially for functional reasons.
evidence: This is a proposal from the authors based on their analysis.

claim: 525 out of 1536 P-TADs have E–P/P–P loops that coincide with their boundaries.
source: The statistical analyses of all the P-TADs observed in the Micro-C contact maps across all the chromosomes show that 525 out of 1536 P-TADs have E–P/P–P loops that coincide with their boundaries (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' analysis of Micro-C data, shown in Figure 8.

claim: The maintenance of E–P/–P–P interactions could be the origin of the P-TADs even if there are no epigenetic switches.
source: Taken together, our observations suggest that the maintenance of E–P/–P–P interactions could be the origin of the P-TADs even if there are no epigenetic switches.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' analysis of Micro-C data.

claim: By analyzing the experimental Hi-C data, we first showed that upon cohesin loss a non-negligible fraction of TADs is preserved, which was not previously noticed.
source: By analyzing the experimental Hi-C data (Rao et al., 2017; Schwarzer et al., 2017), we first showed that upon cohesin loss a non-negligible fraction of TADs is preserved, which was not previously noticed.
evidence: This is a key finding from the authors' analysis of experimental Hi-C data.

claim: The simulations showed that switches in the epigenetic states across the TAD boundary account for a large fraction of P-TADs.
source: The simulations showed that switches in the epigenetic states across the TAD boundary account for a large fraction of P-TADs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' polymer simulations.

claim: Even in the absence of epigenetic switches, P-TADs could be preserved, as revealed by the presence of physical boundaries in the 3D structures.
source: Even in the absence of epigenetic switches, P-TADs could be preserved, as revealed by the presence of physical boundaries in the 3D structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' analysis of 3D structures.

claim: Deletion of cohesin in the GM12878 cell line also leads to P-TADs, a prediction that suggests that P-TADs may be 'universal'.
source: Although not emphasized, we showed that deletion of cohesin in the GM12878 cell line also leads to P-TADs, a prediction that suggests that P-TADs may be 'universal'.
evidence: This is a prediction from the authors' polymer simulations.

claim: P-TADs may be linked to the maintenance of enhancer–promoter and promoter–promoter interactions.
source: (5) Finally, we suggest that P-TADs may be linked to the maintenance of enhancer–promoter and promoter–promoter interactions by calculating the 3D structures using the recent Micro-C data (Hsieh et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a suggestion from the authors based on their analysis of Micro-C data.

claim: The prediction of 3D structures using the HIPPS method does not require extensive polymer simulations.
source: Because the prediction of 3D structures using the HIPPS method does not require extensive polymer simulations, it can be used to predict the structural changes for chromosomes that are subject to large-scale perturbations.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the HIPPS method used by the authors.

claim: The excellent agreement between the HIPPS calculations and imaging experiments further bolsters the power of our approach.
source: The excellent agreement between the HIPPS calculations and imaging experiments further bolsters the power of our approach.
evidence: This is the authors' assessment of the validity of their approach based on comparison with experiments.
